Neonatal Javan short-tailed gymnures are remarkably diminutive, with newborns possessing a wet body mass of merely 1.16 grams [Wwb = 1.16 grams]. This exceptionally low birth weight, which was estimated through comparative scaling relationships derived from the closely related African hedgehog (Atelerix albiventris), places the species among the smallest eutherian neonates relative to adult size. The suckling juveniles depend entirely on maternal milk during the initial weeks of life, and under the stable thermal conditions of the maternal nest, which approximates a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], the young achieve nutritional independence through weaning after a remarkably brief interval of 36 days since birth [tx = 36 days since birth]. This rapid progression from a dependent newborn to a weaned juvenile is a critical developmental phase, representing the transition from reliance on lactation to independent foraging. The altricial neonates are born hairless and with closed eyes, requiring constant maternal attendance, and the relatively short weaning period likely reflects the high metabolic demands placed on the lactating female in the humid, tropical forests of Java. Field observations confirm that the tiny newborns are entirely helpless, clinging to the mother's teats for sustained periods. The speed of this early development has implications for understanding the life history strategy of this insectivorous mammal.

As the weaned juveniles continue their development toward adulthood, they undergo a substantial increase in body mass. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown, reproductively viable adult individuals of Hylomys suillus is approximately 57.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 57.8 grams]. This represents more than a forty-fold increase from the neonatal mass of just over a gram, reflecting a period of intense growth and somatic maturation. The progression from a weaned juvenile to a reproductively mature adult is marked by the onset of puberty, which occurs at 120 days since birth [tp = 120 days since birth] when the animals are maintained at a body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity for a mammal of this body size suggests a fast-paced life history, perhaps adapted to environments with high juvenile mortality or ephemeral resource availability. The growing sub-adults must accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic costs of future reproduction, and the final adult mass of approximately 57.8 grams provides a crucial benchmark for understanding the species' basal metabolic demands and its ecological role as a small, ground-dwelling forager. Field studies indicate that individuals continue to grow slowly even after reaching reproductive maturity.

Reproductive output in the Javan short-tailed gymnure is modest when compared to many other small eutherian mammals of similar body mass. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], and within that single annual reproductive event, they give birth to two to four pups per litter [N_R_i = two to four pups per litter]. This low annual fecundity is unusual for an insectivore of its size, and it suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. The gestation period supporting this limited reproductive output lasts for 30 days [tg = 30 days] at a maternal core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], a relatively short gestational interval that is consistent with the altricial state of the newborns. The tiny pups, weighing only slightly more than a gram each at birth, are born in a highly dependent state following this month-long pregnancy. The low litter size and singular annual reproductive bout may be linked to the energetic constraints of lactation in a tropical environment where insect prey abundance, while consistent, may not support a second costly reproductive effort. This reproductive pattern contrasts sharply with many temperate-zone shrews and hedgehogs that can produce multiple litters within a single favorable season.

The basal metabolic rate of Hylomys suillus has been quantified through respirometry at a resting oxygen consumption of 60.1 milliliters per hour [JOi = 60.1 milliliters per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This peak basal metabolic rate, recorded under thermoneutral conditions, provides a fundamental measure of the energetic cost of living for this small mammal. Compared to other members of the family Erinaceidae, the gymnure's metabolic rate falls within the expected range for an insectivorous mammal of its approximately 57.8 gram adult body mass, though it is notably higher than that of the more derived, spiny hedgehogs which often exhibit lower metabolic rates as an adaptation to temperate climates. The maintenance of a stable core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] in the humid lowland and montane forests of Java likely imposes a significant daily energetic burden, necessitating a nearly constant foraging effort to meet metabolic demands. This high resting metabolism is consistent with the species' active, ground-dwelling lifestyle and its reliance on a protein-rich diet of invertebrates. The 60.1 milliliters per hour value represents the maximum sustainable metabolic rate under basal conditions, providing a crucial reference point for understanding the species' ecological energetics.

The life history of Hylomys suillus is further defined by its longevity, with a maximum lifespan in the wild documented at 730 days [am = 730 days] under natural thermal conditions approximating 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This lifespan of approximately two years is relatively short, even for a small mammal, and it aligns with the species' rapid developmental schedule and modest annual reproductive output. The physiological deterioration associated with senescence in these gymnures remains poorly documented in the primary literature. This combination of life history traits—fast development, low fecundity, and a short lifespan—positions the Javan short-tailed gymnure as an intriguing outlier among tropical insectivores.
